config.title: Lifting State Up

intro.title: Lifting State Up
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple temperature converter that allows you to switch between Celsius and Fahrenheit. You will learn the concept of 'lifting state up,' which means moving shared state to the closest common parent component so multiple child components can use and update it. The main technologies involved are React functional components, TypeScript for type safety, and the useState hook for managing state. This approach helps keep your components synchronized and your code easier to maintain.
intro.usecase: Lifting state up is essential when multiple UI components need to share and synchronize data. In e-commerce sites, product filters (category, price range, ratings) must update the displayed product list simultaneously. Dashboard applications use this pattern when date range selectors control multiple charts and data tables. Form wizards also rely on lifted state to maintain user input across multiple steps while enabling validation and submission logic in a parent component.

objectives: Implement a parent component that manages shared state for multiple child components
Configure child components to receive state values as props from a parent
Construct callback functions in a parent component to update lifted state
Bind event handlers in child components to parent-provided callback props
Update TypeScript interfaces to define props for components sharing lifted state
Render sibling components that synchronize their display through shared parent state
Manipulate a single source of truth for related UI elements by lifting state

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: You'll need both React and the useState hook for state management in this lesson.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported React and useState correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the parent TemperatureConverter component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TemperatureConverter that returns an empty fragment (<></>) for now.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function with the name TemperatureConverter and have it return an empty fragment.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the TemperatureConverter component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A TemperatureConverter component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: The TemperatureConverter component is created and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named TemperatureConverter that returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created a functional component named TemperatureConverter with an empty fragment return.

steps.title: Define the temperature state in the parent component
steps.instruction: Inside your TemperatureConverter component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'temperature' initialized to 0, with its setter function.
steps.hint: Remember to destructure useState to get the state variable and setter function. The state variable should be named 'temperature' and initialized to 0.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureConverter component now has a state variable 'temperature' initialized to 0, ready to be shared with child components.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with initial value 0, and the destructured variables are named 'temperature' and 'setTemperature'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've named the state variable 'temperature' and initialized it to 0 with useState.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the TemperatureConverter component, use useState to create a state variable called 'temperature' with initial value 0.

steps.title: Create the CelsiusInput child component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named CelsiusInput that accepts temperature and onTemperatureChange as props.
steps.hint: Define a new component function that takes props as an argument. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a new CelsiusInput component defined that accepts temperature and onTemperatureChange props.
successCriteria: A component named CelsiusInput is created with props for temperature and onTemperatureChange.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your CelsiusInput component accepts both temperature and onTemperatureChange as props.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CelsiusInput component isn't properly defined. Create a functional component named CelsiusInput that accepts temperature and onTemperatureChange as props.

steps.title: Define TypeScript interface for CelsiusInput props
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named 'CelsiusInputProps' with two properties: 'temperature' of type 'number' and 'onTemperatureChange' of type '(value: number) => void'.
steps.hint: Define the interface above the CelsiusInput component using the 'interface' keyword.
steps.expectedOutcome: The interface is defined with the correct property types, ready to be used as the props type for the CelsiusInput component.
successCriteria: The interface 'CelsiusInputProps' is defined with 'temperature: number' and 'onTemperatureChange: (value: number) => void' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both properties are included with the correct types: 'temperature' should be 'number' and 'onTemperatureChange' should be a function type that takes a number and returns void.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword and include both required properties with proper TypeScript types.

steps.title: Create the FahrenheitInput child component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named FahrenheitInput that accepts the same props interface as CelsiusInput and returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a new component with the same structure as CelsiusInput but named FahrenheitInput.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new FahrenheitInput component is defined with the correct props type.
successCriteria: FahrenheitInput component exists, accepts CelsiusInputProps, and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component is named FahrenheitInput and accepts CelsiusInputProps.
steps.feedbackWrong: The FahrenheitInput component is missing or has incorrect props.

steps.title: Implement the temperature conversion handler in parent
steps.instruction: Inside the TemperatureConverter component, define a function named handleTemperatureChange that takes a number parameter and updates the temperature state.
steps.hint: The function should accept a temperature value (number) and call setTemperature with that value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleTemperatureChange function is defined in the parent component that updates the temperature state.
successCriteria: The handleTemperatureChange function is defined with a number parameter and calls setTemperature.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function accepts a number parameter and calls setTemperature with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. It should take a number and update the temperature state using setTemperature.

steps.title: Render child components in parent with props
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your TemperatureConverter component, render both the CelsiusInput and FahrenheitInput components, passing the temperature state and handleTemperatureChange function as props.
steps.hint: You need to call each component like a JSX element (<CelsiusInput />) and pass props to them. The props should match the interfaces you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The parent component's return statement now includes both child components with the temperature state and handler function passed as props.
successCriteria: Both CelsiusInput and FahrenheitInput components are rendered in the parent's return statement with temperature and handleTemperatureChange passed as props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're passing both props (temperature and handleTemperatureChange) to both child components. Check that the prop names match what the child components expect.
steps.feedbackWrong: The child components aren't properly rendered with props. Remember to include both <CelsiusInput /> and <FahrenheitInput /> in the return statement, passing temperature and handleTemperatureChange as props to each.

steps.title: Implement CelsiusInput component markup
steps.instruction: In the CelsiusInput component, return an input field with type='number', value set to props.temperature, and onChange wired to props.onTemperatureChange.
steps.hint: The input should be a controlled component that receives its value and change handler from props.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CelsiusInput component renders a controlled number input that displays the temperature value and calls the parent's change handler when edited.
successCriteria: CelsiusInput returns an <input> element with type='number', value={props.temperature}, and onChange that calls props.onTemperatureChange with the parsed number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the input has type='number', value is set to props.temperature, and onChange calls props.onTemperatureChange with the parsed number from e.target.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CelsiusInput component doesn't yet render the required input field. Check that you're returning an <input> element with the correct attributes.

steps.title: Implement FahrenheitInput component with conversion
steps.instruction: Create the FahrenheitInput functional component that accepts the same props interface as CelsiusInput, converts the temperature prop to Fahrenheit, and returns an input field with the converted value.
steps.hint: Define the component to receive temperature and onTemperatureChange props, calculate Fahrenheit using (temperature * 9/5) + 32, and return an input element with value set to the Fahrenheit calculation.
steps.expectedOutcome: The FahrenheitInput component is defined with proper TypeScript props, converts Celsius to Fahrenheit, and returns an input element ready for event handling.
successCriteria: FahrenheitInput component is created with the correct props interface, temperature conversion formula is implemented, and an input element with value attribute is returned.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the FahrenheitInput component, but make sure to include the temperature conversion formula and return an input element with the calculated value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The FahrenheitInput component is missing or incomplete. Remember to create a functional component that accepts temperature and onTemperatureChange props, converts to Fahrenheit, and returns an input element.
